name: Lotus extract
lead: Lotus extract is derived from the sacred lotus (Nelumbo nucifera), an aquatic perennial whose seeds, rhizomes and leaves have long been used in food and in folk, Ayurvedic and Chinese medicine.[1] It appears as an antioxidant botanical in K-beauty and other skincare products. The name is also applied to unrelated plants such as blue lotus (Nymphaea caerulea), which has different chemistry.[2]

Human evidence is small. Two 2013 studies tested topical formulations of green tea and lotus extract on facial wrinkles and sebum in small groups of healthy adults.[3][4] Other lotus research is in animals or the laboratory.[5]

paras: Sacred lotus has been cultivated for food for about 3,000 years. Reported constituents include flavonols such as miquelianin and benzylisoquinoline alkaloids such as nuciferine and neferine in leaves, and proteins, polyphenols and polysaccharides in seeds.[1] Wikipedia notes that medical claims about the plant need more reliable references.[1]
Lotus extract is used in serums and creams for its antioxidant content. In the studies below it was combined with green tea extract in multiple-emulsion formulations.[3][4]
A 2013 study evaluated green tea and lotus extract formulations for facial wrinkles in 33 healthy Asian men using a skin imaging device (Visioscan VC and SELS software).[3]

A 2013 single-blinded, placebo-controlled, split-face study with 22 healthy adults compared green tea and green tea plus lotus emulsions against placebo for sebum control.[4] Both studies tested lotus in combination with green tea, small samples, and cosmetic endpoints. No large independent trials were found.

A water extract of lotus seed was reported to promote non-REM sleep in rats via GABAergic receptors.[5] An ethanolic extract of lotus leaves showed iron-chelating and anti-hemolytic properties in laboratory work.[6] A 2023 survey and safety assessment of blue lotus (Nymphaea caerulea) extracts examined a different species sold as extracts.[2]

card.summary: Sacred-lotus botanical in K-beauty skincare; only two small human studies exist, both paired with green tea.
card.note: Do not confuse with blue lotus (Nymphaea), a different plant.

quick.overview:
Lotus extract comes from the sacred lotus and is used in skincare as an antioxidant ingredient.

Two small 2013 studies tested lotus combined with green tea on wrinkles and oiliness.
quick.mechanism: It is proposed to act through antioxidant flavonoids and related plant compounds.
quick.risks: No specific cosmetic safety problems were identified in the sources reviewed. Blue lotus extracts are a different product with their own safety assessment.
